claims.claim: Over-expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap increases leader bleb area compared to over-expression of Emerald-mEps8.
claims.source: Over-expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap similarly increased leader bleb area compared to over-expression of Emerald-mEps8 (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 1B.

claims.claim: Unlike the gradient of Emerald-mEps8 with the highest level at the leader bleb base, Emerald-mEps8Δcap is equally distributed along the length of the leader bleb or slightly concentrated at the tip.
claims.source: Confocal imaging of confined Eps8-KD cells and analysis of re-expressed protein distribution together with FusionRed-F-tractin or -MII-RLC showed that unlike the gradient of Emerald-mEps8 with the highest level at the leader bleb base, Emerald-mEps8Δcap was equally distributed along the length of the leader bleb or slightly concentrated at the tip (Figure 5E,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 5E and 5G.

claims.claim: Expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap in Eps8-KD cells decreases the level of actin in the dense cortical band of the cell body compared to expression of Emerald-mEps8.
claims.source: Analysis of actomyosin organization showed that compared to expression of Emerald-mEps8, expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap in Eps8-KD cells decreased the level of actin in the dense cortical band of the cell body, although the density gradient of actin along the leader bleb and the distribution of MII-RLC was unchanged (Figure 5E,F,G′ and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5E, 5F, 5G′, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap in Eps8-KD cells does not change the density gradient of actin along the leader bleb or the distribution of MII-RLC.
claims.source: Analysis of actomyosin organization showed that compared to expression of Emerald-mEps8, expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap in Eps8-KD cells decreased the level of actin in the dense cortical band of the cell body, although the density gradient of actin along the leader bleb and the distribution of MII-RLC was unchanged (Figure 5E,F,G′ and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5E, 5F, 5G′, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The actin bundle anisotropy gradient in the leader bleb is highly enhanced in Eps8-KD cells expressing Emerald-mEps8Δcap, with nearly fivefold higher actin bundle anisotropy near the tips of their leader blebs compared to Eps8-KD cells expressing Emerald-mEps8.
claims.source: In contrast, the actin bundle anisotropy gradient in the leader bleb was highly enhanced, with Eps8-KD cells expressing Emerald-mEps8Δcap exhibiting nearly fivefold higher actin bundle anisotropy near the tips of their leader blebs compared to Eps8-KD cells expressing Emerald-mEps8 (Figure 5G″).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5G″.

claims.claim: Over-expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap significantly increases cortex tension and intracellular pressure compared to over-expression of Emerald-mEps8.
claims.source: AFM analysis of cortex mechanics showed that compared to over-expression of Emerald-mEps8, over-expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap significantly increased cortex tension and intracellular pressure (Figure 5H–I and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5H-I and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The capping activity of Eps8 decreases actin density and mechanical properties of the cortex in the cell body.
claims.source: Together, these results show that the capping activity of Eps8 decreases actin density and mechanical properties of the cortex in the cell body, but acts to antagonize actin bundle formation in the distal region of leader blebs, and together this limits leader bleb size.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the capping-defective mutant decreases cortical actin density and increases mechanical properties.

claims.claim: The capping activity of Eps8 acts to antagonize actin bundle formation in the distal region of leader blebs.
claims.source: Together, these results show that the capping activity of Eps8 decreases actin density and mechanical properties of the cortex in the cell body, but acts to antagonize actin bundle formation in the distal region of leader blebs, and together this limits leader bleb size.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the capping-defective mutant enhances actin bundle anisotropy at the leader bleb tip.

claims.claim: The capping activity of Eps8 limits leader bleb size.
claims.source: Together, these results show that the capping activity of Eps8 decreases actin density and mechanical properties of the cortex in the cell body, but acts to antagonize actin bundle formation in the distal region of leader blebs, and together this limits leader bleb size.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the capping-defective mutant increases leader bleb size.

claims.claim: The capping activity of Eps8 may be regionally regulated to maintain a gradient of actin bundle organization in the leader bleb.
claims.source: This further suggests that the capping activity of Eps8 may be regionally regulated to maintain a gradient of actin bundle organization in the leader bleb.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that the capping-defective mutant alters the distribution of Eps8 and actin bundle organization in leader blebs.

claims.claim: Erk-dependent phosphorylation of Eps8 on S624 and T628 inhibits actin capping by Eps8 without altering its filament binding activity.
claims.source: Erk-dependent phosphorylation of Eps8 on S624 and T628 has been shown to inhibit actin capping by Eps8 without altering its filament binding activity (Menna et al., 2009), and our above results suggest that capping may be regionally regulated in melanoma cells migrating under non-adhesive confinement.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Menna et al., 2009.

claims.claim: U0126 inhibits Eps8 phosphorylation in A375 cells.
claims.source: We validated that U0126 inhibited Eps8 phosphorylation in A375 cells by expressing either Emerald-mEps8 or EGFP as a control in cells treated with or without 10 μM U0126 for 90 min, performing immunoprecipitation of the expressed proteins with anti-GFP antibodies from cell lysates, followed by western blot analysis with antibodies specific to Erk, activated Erk phosphorylated on T202/Y204, or phospho-serine and phospho-threonine (pS/T). This analysis showed, as expected, that U0126 inhibited Erk activation independent of the expression of Eps8 constructs. Similarly, U0126 strongly reduced the pS/T level in immunoprecipitated Emerald-mEps8 compared to untreated cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data described in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: U0126 treatment causes A375 cells to flatten out at their base, form actin bundles in the cell center and lamellipodia and filopodia with Eps8 on their tips, although they still possess small blebs containing Eps8 on their dorsal surface.
claims.source: This showed that U0126 treatment caused cells to flatten out at their base where they attached to the coverslip and to form actin bundles in the cell center and lamellipodia and filopodia with Eps8 on their tips, although they still possessed small blebs containing Eps8 on their dorsal surface (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Perfusion of U0126 to confined cells co-expressing FusionRed-F-tractin and EGFP-MII-RLC induces rapid retraction of leader blebs and formation of actin bundles in the center of the cell body that lack myosin II.
claims.source: When cells co-expressing FusionRed-F-tractin and EGFP-MII-RLC were confined under non-adherent conditions and perfused with U0126, this remarkably induced rapid retraction of leader blebs and formation of actin bundles in the center of the cell body that lacked myosin II (Figure 6C and Video 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C and Video 6.

claims.claim: U0126 significantly reduces leader bleb area and density of the cortical actin band in the cell body compared to untreated control.
claims.source: Quantification showed that compared to untreated control, U0126 significantly reduced leader bleb area and density of the cortical actin band in the cell body, and completely blocked leader-bleb based migration (Figure 6D,E,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D, 6E, and 6F.

claims.claim: U0126 completely blocks leader-bleb based migration.
claims.source: Quantification showed that compared to untreated control, U0126 significantly reduced leader bleb area and density of the cortical actin band in the cell body, and completely blocked leader-bleb based migration (Figure 6D,E,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D, 6E, and 6F.

claims.claim: U0126 reduces both cortical tension and intracellular pressure compared to control.
claims.source: AFM analysis of cortical mechanics showed that U0126 reduced both cortical tension and intracellular pressure compared to control (Figure 6G–H and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 6G-H and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Erk activity mediates spatial regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, promoting actin density in the cortex and inhibiting actin bundling in the cell center.
claims.source: These results illustrate two important points. First, they show that Erk activity mediates spatial regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, such that it promotes actin density in the cortex and inhibits actin bundling in the cell center.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that Erk inhibition reduces cortical actin density and induces central actin bundles.

claims.claim: Erk activity is required for maintaining cortical tension and intracellular pressure to drive leader bleb formation for adhesion-independent migration under confinement.
claims.source: Second, Erk activity is required for maintaining cortical tension and intracellular pressure to drive leader bleb formation for adhesion-independent migration under confinement.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that Erk inhibition reduces cortical tension, intracellular pressure, and leader bleb formation.

claims.claim: Either reconstitution of Eps8-KD or over-expression with Emerald-mEps8-SATA blocks leader bleb formation, significantly reducing leader bleb size by approximately 50% and strongly inhibiting cell migration compared to expression of Emerald-mEps8 in either wild type or Eps8-KD cells.
claims.source: This showed that either reconstitution of Eps8-KD or over-expression with Emerald-mEps8-SATA blocked leader bleb formation, significantly reducing leader bleb size by ∼50% and strongly inhibiting cell migration compared to expression of Emerald-mEps8 in either wild type or Eps8-KD cells (Figure 7A–D, Supplementary file 1 and Video 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7A-D, Supplementary file 1, and Video 7.

claims.claim: S624 and T628 in Eps8 are required for leader bleb formation and migration under non-adhesive confinement.
claims.source: Thus, S624 and T628 in Eps8 are required for leader bleb formation and migration under non-adhesive confinement.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the non-phosphorylatable mutant blocks leader bleb formation and migration.

claims.claim: Down-regulation of capping activity by phosphorylation at S624 and T628 promotes leader blebs.
claims.source: This further suggests that down-regulation of capping activity by phosphorylation at these sites promotes leader blebs, in agreement with our finding that the capping-deficient Eps8Δcap enhances leader blebs.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the non-phosphorylatable mutant blocks leader blebs, consistent with the capping-deficient mutant enhancing leader blebs.

claims.claim: Emerald-mEps8-SATA forms thick bundle structures in the cell center that are not labeled with F-tractin.
claims.source: Interestingly, expression of Emerald-mEps8-SATA together with FusionRed-F-tractin showed that the Eps8 phospho-mutant was depleted from the cortex and instead formed thick bundle structures in the cell center (Figure 7E), similar to the actin bundles seen in cells treated with U0126 (Figure 6C), but the bundles were not labeled with F-tractin (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The Emerald-mEps8-SATA cables are dense with actin and do not co-localize with intermediate filaments.
claims.source: However, fixation and staining with antibodies to vimentin or with fluorescent phalloidin showed that the Emerald-mEps8-SATA cables did not co-localize with intermediate filaments, but were dense with actin, suggesting that F-tractin and Eps8 may compete for the same binding site in actin bundles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: F-tractin and Eps8 may compete for the same binding site in actin bundles.
claims.source: However, fixation and staining with antibodies to vimentin or with fluorescent phalloidin showed that the Emerald-mEps8-SATA cables did not co-localize with intermediate filaments, but were dense with actin, suggesting that F-tractin and Eps8 may compete for the same binding site in actin bundles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that F-tractin does not label Eps8-SATA bundles despite them being dense with actin.

claims.claim: Emerald-mEps8-SATA does not alter actin density in the cortical band of the cell body compared to Emerald-mEps8.
claims.source: Analysis of fluorescent phalloidin intensity in the cortical band of the cell body showed that Emerald-mEps8-SATA did not alter actin density compared to Emerald-mEps8 (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The central Eps8/actin bundles formed by Emerald-mEps8-SATA lack myosin II.
claims.source: In addition, co-expression of Emerald-mEps8-SATA together with FusionRed MII-RLC in Eps8-KD cells showed that myosin II continued to localize to the peripheral cortex, but the central Eps8/actin bundles lacked myosin II (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Over-expression of Emerald-mEps8 or Emerald-mEps8-SATA induces bundles in approximately 30% or approximately 70% of cells, respectively.
claims.source: Quantification of the percentage of cells with Eps8/actin bundles showed that expression of F-tractin did not induce bundle formation, while over-expression of Emerald-mEps8 or Emerald-mEps8-SATA induced bundles in ∼30% or ∼70% of cells, respectively (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7H.

claims.claim: Emerald-mEps8-SATA promotes the formation of excessive non-contractile actin bundles in the cell center.
claims.source: This indicates that Emerald-mEps8-SATA promotes the formation of excessive non-contractile actin bundles in the cell center.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that Emerald-mEps8-SATA induces central actin bundles that lack myosin II.

claims.claim: The S624 and T628 Erk phosphorylation sites in Eps8 are required for suppressing central actin bundles.
claims.source: Together with our previous results, this suggests that the S624 and T628 Erk phosphorylation sites in Eps8, are required for suppressing central actin bundles, while other targets of MEK/Erk regulate cortical actin density.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the non-phosphorylatable mutant induces central actin bundles.

claims.claim: Other targets of MEK/Erk regulate cortical actin density.
claims.source: Together with our previous results, this suggests that the S624 and T628 Erk phosphorylation sites in Eps8, are required for suppressing central actin bundles, while other targets of MEK/Erk regulate cortical actin density.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that Erk inhibition reduces cortical actin density but the non-phosphorylatable Eps8 mutant does not.

claims.claim: Erk inhibition induces Eps8/actin cables to the same extent, independent of the S624A/T628A mutations.
claims.source: Treatment of non-adherent cells expressing either Emerald-mEps8 or Emerald-mEps8-SATA with 10 μM U0126 for 90 min followed by fixation and phalloidin staining showed that Erk inhibition induced Eps8/actin cables to the same extent, independent of the S624A/T628A mutations (Figure 7G,H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7G and 7H.

claims.claim: Both capping and bundling activities are required for cable formation induced by Erk inhibition.
claims.source: Over-expression of either Emerald-mEps8Δcap or Emerald-mEps8Δbund in either the presence or absence of U0126 did not induce Eps8/actin cables, indicating that both capping and bundling activities are required for cable formation induced by Erk inhibition (Figure 7G,H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7G and 7H.

claims.claim: Over-expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap in cells treated with U0126 and confined under agar cannot rescue the loss of leader blebs induced by perfusion of Erk inhibitor.
claims.source: Furthermore, over-expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap in cells treated with U0126 and confined under agar could not rescue the loss of leader blebs induced by perfusion of Erk inhibitor (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), indicating that Erk promotes leader blebs by other mechanisms in addition to down-regulation of Eps8 capping activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Erk promotes leader blebs by other mechanisms in addition to down-regulation of Eps8 capping activity.
claims.source: Furthermore, over-expression of Emerald-mEps8Δcap in cells treated with U0126 and confined under agar could not rescue the loss of leader blebs induced by perfusion of Erk inhibitor (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), indicating that Erk promotes leader blebs by other mechanisms in addition to down-regulation of Eps8 capping activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the capping-deficient mutant cannot rescue the effects of Erk inhibition.

claims.claim: MEK/Erk-mediated phosphorylation of Eps8 on S624 and T628 inhibits the bundling- and capping-dependent formation of central actin cables by Eps8.
claims.source: However, together our results show that MEK/Erk-mediated phosphorylation of Eps8 on S624 and T628 inhibits the bundling- and capping-dependent formation of central actin cables by Eps8.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the non-phosphorylatable mutant induces central actin cables and that both capping and bundling activities are required for cable formation.

claims.claim: In addition to directly regulating actin capping, S624 and T628 may affect the bundling activity of Eps8 in cells by an indirect mechanism.
claims.source: This also suggests that in addition to directly regulating actin capping (Menna et al., 2009), these sites may affect the bundling activity of Eps8 in cells by an indirect mechanism.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that the non-phosphorylatable mutant affects both capping and bundling-dependent processes.

claims.claim: Emerald-mEps8-SATA expression reduces cortex tension and intracellular pressure to a level similar to treatment with U0126 compared to untreated or cells expressing Emerald-mEps8.
claims.source: AFM analysis showed that compared to untreated or cells expressing Emerald-mEps8, Emerald-mEps8-SATA expression reduced cortex tension and intracellular pressure to a level similar to treatment with U0126 (Figures 7I,J, 6G,H and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figures 7I, 7J, 6G, 6H, and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Erk-mediated phosphorylation of S624 and T628 coordinates the local co-regulation of Eps8 capping and bundling activities to control cortical tension and intracellular pressure to mediate leader bleb formation and migration of confined cells.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that Erk-mediated phosphorylation of S624 and T628 coordinates the local co-regulation of Eps8 capping and bundling activities to control cortical tension and intracellular pressure to mediate leader bleb formation and migration of confined cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the non-phosphorylatable mutant affects cortical tension, intracellular pressure, and leader bleb formation.

claims.claim: In cells adhered to fibronectin-coated glass, EKAREV is soluble, excluded from membranous organelles, and diffusely localized throughout the cell, with a low FRET signal indicating low Erk activity throughout the cell.
claims.source: Confocal imaging showed that EKAREV (CFP channel) was soluble, excluded from membranous organelles, and diffusely localized throughout the cell, while YFP/CFP ratio imaging revealed a low FRET signal indicating low Erk activity throughout the cell (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: In non-adherent, blebbing cells, the EKAREV reporter is evenly distributed, but the ratio image shows heightened levels of FRET indicating higher Erk activity specifically in blebs.
claims.source: In contrast, in non-adherent, blebbing cells, although the EKAREV reporter was evenly distributed, the ratio image showed heightened levels of FRET indicating higher Erk activity specifically in blebs (Figure 8B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claims.claim: Treatment with U0126 reduces the EKAREV FRET ratio to minimal levels.
claims.source: Importantly, treatment with U0126 reduced the EKAREV FRET ratio to minimal levels (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A flash of high FRET appears in the bleb periphery just after protrusion and is maintained until bleb retraction.
claims.source: Remarkably, time-lapse ratio imaging at 5 s intervals showed that a flash of high FRET appeared in the bleb periphery just after protrusion, and was maintained until bleb retraction (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: EKAREV reveals spatially and temporally localized Erk activity in blebs of non-adherent cells.
claims.source: Thus, EKAREV reveals spatially and temporally localized Erk activity in blebs of non-adherent cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the EKAREV imaging data.

claims.claim: In non-adherent cells confined under agarose, there is a strong concentration of high FRET signal indicating high Erk activity within leader blebs compared to the cell body.
claims.source: Strikingly, confocal YFP/CFP ratio imaging revealed a strong concentration of high FRET signal indicating high Erk activity within leader blebs compared to the cell body (Figure 8D and Video 8).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8D and Video 8.

claims.claim: There is greater than 250% enrichment of Erk activity in the leader bleb relative to the cell body.
claims.source: Quantification of the magnitude of FRET signal in the leader bleb relative to the cell body showed >250% enrichment of Erk activity in the leader bleb (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: Regional analysis of the magnitude of FRET signal distribution within leader blebs shows a shallow gradient, with Erk activity highest at the distal tip.
claims.source: Furthermore, regional analysis of the magnitude of FRET signal distribution within leader blebs showed a shallow gradient, with Erk activity highest at the distal tip (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: EGFP alone and EKAREV are enriched by approximately 10-12% in the leader bleb relative to the cell body.
claims.source: Quantification showed that EGFP alone as well as EKAREV were enriched by ∼10–12% in the leader bleb relative to the cell body (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: Erk, MEK and B-Raf (V600E) are all enriched within leader blebs by 15-20% relative to the cell body.
claims.source: Although Erk, MEK and B-Raf (V600E) were all enriched within leader blebs by 15–20% relative to the cell body (Figure 8F,G), this was not significantly higher than the enrichment of EGFP alone.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8F and 8G.

claims.claim: Slight enrichment of soluble proteins within leader blebs may be a general phenomenon, likely because membranous organelles that exclude cytoplasmic markers are largely excluded from the leader bleb and maintained in the cell body.
claims.source: Therefore, slight enrichment of soluble proteins within leader blebs may be a general phenomenon, likely because membranous organelles that exclude cytoplasmic markers are largely excluded from the leader bleb and maintained in the cell body.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that soluble proteins are slightly enriched in leader blebs.

claims.claim: In confined non-adherent cells, Erk activity is highly concentrated in leader blebs where it forms a gradient with peak activity at the bleb tip.
claims.source: Together, our results show that in confined non-adherent cells, Erk activity is highly concentrated in leader blebs where it forms a gradient with peak activity at the bleb tip.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the EKAREV imaging data.

claims.claim: The majority of red fluorescence from photo-converted mEos is retained within and diffuses throughout the leader bleb before equilibrating with the cell body.
claims.source: This showed that the majority of the red fluorescence was retained within and diffused throughout the leader bleb before equilibrating with the cell body (Figure 8H and Video 9).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8H and Video 9.

claims.claim: The bleb neck slows diffusion of soluble components between the leader bleb and cell body.
claims.source: These results indicate that the bleb neck slows diffusion of soluble components between the leader bleb and cell body.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the mEos2 photo-conversion data.

claims.claim: Erk activity concentrates in and forms a gradient across leader blebs, and may be trapped there by a diffusion barrier at the bleb neck.
claims.source: Together, these results show that Erk activity concentrates in and forms a gradient across leader blebs, and may be trapped there by a diffusion barrier at the bleb neck.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the EKAREV and mEos2 data.

claims.claim: Eps8 plays a critical role in promoting cell cortex tension and intracellular pressure to induce the rapid, adhesion-independent migration of confined cancer cells.
claims.source: Our study shows for the first time a critical role for Eps8 and its regulation of the actin cytoskeleton in promoting cell cortex tension and intracellular pressure to induce the rapid, adhesion-independent migration of confined cancer cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claims.claim: In non-adherent melanoma cells, Eps8 localizes to bleb membranes as actin assembles.
claims.source: We demonstrate that, in contrast to cells adhered to ECM where Eps8 associates with filopodia and lamellipodia, in non-adherent melanoma cells, Eps8 localizes to bleb membranes as actin assembles.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary of the imaging data showing Eps8 localization in non-adherent cells.

claims.claim: Eps8 is required to promote the mesenchymal-to-leader bleb transition under confinement by enhancing cortical tension and promoting increased intracellular pressure.
claims.source: We show here that in cancer cells, the actin capping and bundling scaffold protein Eps8 is required to promote this morphological transition under confinement by enhancing cortical tension and promoting increased intracellular pressure.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claims.claim: Both contractility and proper organization of the cytoskeleton are critical to generating the cortical mechanical properties conducive to leader bleb-based migration under non-adhesive confinement.
claims.source: This, together with previous work (Bergert et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Ruprecht et al., 2015), indicates that both contractility and proper organization of the cytoskeleton are critical to generating the cortical mechanical properties conducive to leader bleb-based migration under non-adhesive confinement.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of previous work.

claims.claim: The bundling activity of Eps8 is critical to promoting the cortical inhomogeneity and cellular pressure that mediate symmetry breaking to drive the polarized cell shape change to leader bleb morphology.
claims.source: We find that the bundling activity of Eps8 is required for promoting the mesenchymal-to-leader bleb transition in confined, non-adherent melanoma cells. This identifies a critical role for actin bundles in promoting the cortical inhomogeneity and cellular pressure that have been postulated to mediate symmetry breaking to drive this drastic polarized cell shape change (Ruprecht et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of a cited study on symmetry breaking.

claims.claim: Eps8's bundling and capping activities act antagonistically, such that when capping is down-regulated, Eps8 may be a more efficient bundler.
claims.source: Our demonstration that inhibition of Eps8 capping activity further enhances actin bundle organization towards the leading bleb tip suggests that Eps8's bundling and capping activities act antagonistically, such that when capping is down-regulated, Eps8 may be a more efficient bundler.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the capping-deficient mutant enhances actin bundle organization.

claims.claim: Local regulation of Eps8 capping activity could promote polarization of actin organization with opposing gradients in actin density and bundling along the leader bleb.
claims.source: Thus, local regulation of Eps8 capping activity could promote polarization of actin organization with opposing gradients in actin density and bundling along the leader bleb.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that Eps8 capping and bundling activities act antagonistically.

claims.claim: Erk-mediated phosphorylation of S624 and T628 not only down-regulates the capping activity of Eps8 but may coordinate the regulation of Eps8 capping and bundling activities.
claims.source: However, by manipulating Erk activity or the Erk phosphorylation sites in Eps8, we demonstrate that Erk-mediated phosphorylation of S624 and T628 not only down-regulates the capping activity of Eps8 as shown previously (Menna et al., 2009), but may in fact coordinate the regulation of Eps8 capping and bundling activities.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data showing that the non-phosphorylatable mutant affects both capping and bundling-dependent processes.

claims.claim: Erk-mediated down-regulation of Eps8 capping activity at the leader bleb tip could drive the formation of opposing gradients in actin bundling and density along the bleb length.
claims.source: This suggests that Erk-mediated down-regulation of Eps8 capping activity at the leader bleb tip could drive the formation of opposing gradients in actin bundling and density along the bleb length.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that Erk activity is highest at the leader bleb tip.

claims.claim: The gradient in actin organization may be required for spatial organization of cortical tension to maintain the allantoid shape and drive cortical flow in the leader bleb.
claims.source: This gradient in actin organization, in turn, may be required for spatial organization of cortical tension, which we predict would mirror the gradient in actin bundling, to maintain the allantoid shape and drive cortical flow in the leader bleb.

claims.claim: The increased cortical tension at the bleb tip would be opposed at the bleb neck by myosin II contractility, and the depletion of myosin II and actin from the very tip of the leader bleb would provide a site where high intracellular pressure could promote local protrusion of the leading membrane to mediate leader-bleb-based migration.

results.result: Eps8 localizes differentially in adherent versus non-adherent A375 cells. In adherent cells on fibronectin, Eps8 localizes to lamellipodia and arcs but not stress fibers. In non-adherent cells, Eps8 is absent from the dense cortical band but localizes with actin in punctae along bleb peripheries, appearing on a similar timescale as ezrin (~5 seconds after bleb formation) and before myosin II (~30 seconds).
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C8 and C110 are supported by direct imaging data (Figure 1A-H, Figure 1—figure supplements) showing Eps8 localization patterns in different cellular contexts. Time-lapse imaging provides quantitative timing data for protein recruitment to blebs. The observations are internally consistent and well-documented with multiple imaging modalities.

results.result: Under non-adhesive confinement, A375 cells form a single large 'leader bleb' characterized by a sausage shape with a thin neck. Approximately 40% of confined cells migrate rapidly (1.15 ± 1.02 µm/min) in the direction of the leader bleb, while adherent cells do not migrate. Within leader blebs, Eps8 and F-actin are concentrated and form opposing gradients: Eps8 is highest at the neck and lowest at the tip, while actin bundles are most aligned distally. Myosin II is concentrated at the neck and nearly absent from the distal bleb.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C17 are supported by extensive imaging data (Figure 1I-N, Videos 1-3) and quantitative measurements. The morphological descriptions are consistent across multiple experiments. Migration speed measurements include error estimates. The gradient analyses are quantified using regional ROI measurements. The spatial distributions of Eps8, actin, and myosin II are well-documented.

results.result: Eps8 is required for leader bleb formation and migration in A375 cells. siRNA-mediated depletion of Eps8 (76 ± 2.1%) inhibits large leader bleb formation, reduces leader bleb area by nearly half, and reduces the fraction of migrating cells by nearly half. These defects are fully rescued by re-expression of mouse Eps8.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 are supported by Western blot validation of knockdown efficiency (Figure 2A), imaging data showing phenotypic effects (Figure 2B-D), and rescue experiments (Figure 2C-D, Supplementary file 1A). The rescue with mouse Eps8 (which is not targeted by human-specific siRNA) provides strong evidence for specificity. Statistical significance is demonstrated.

results.result: Eps8 depletion causes a slight but significant reduction in cortical actin density in the cell body but does not affect actin density or distribution within leader blebs. However, Eps8-KD makes actin bundle organization highly variable along blebs, disrupting the normal anisotropy gradient. Myosin II localization and activity (pS19 MLC) are unchanged by Eps8 depletion, indicating that Eps8 promotes leader blebs and actin bundling independent of myosin II activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C31 are supported by quantitative imaging analyses (Figure 2E-H) and Western blotting (Figure 2I). The use of FibrilTool for anisotropy measurements provides objective quantification of bundle organization. The finding that myosin II activity is unchanged is important for mechanistic interpretation and is supported by both imaging and biochemical data.

results.result: Eps8 promotes cortex tension and intracellular pressure. AFM measurements show that Eps8-KD significantly decreases both cortex tension and intracellular pressure, though not as strongly as blebbistatin treatment. These effects are rescued by re-expression of Emerald-mEps8. Blebbistatin reduces cortex tension and intracellular pressure without affecting cell radius or cortical actin thickness.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by AFM data (Figure 3C-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1). The methodology is validated using blebbistatin as a positive control, consistent with prior literature (Tinevez et al., 2009). The rescue experiments provide specificity. Statistical significance is demonstrated. The measurements of cell radius and cortex thickness provide important controls.

results.result: The actin bundling activity of Eps8 is required for leader bleb formation and cortical mechanics. A bundling-defective mutant (Emerald-mEps8Δbund, L757A/K759A) localizes to blebs but fails to rescue leader bleb size or migration in Eps8-KD cells and reduces migration by >50%. Over-expression in wild-type cells acts as a dominant negative, likely through dimerization. The bundling-defective mutant significantly reduces cortex tension and intracellular pressure without affecting cortical actin density or myosin II organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C47 are supported by imaging data (Figure 4B-F, Video 4), quantitative measurements of leader bleb area and migration (Figure 4C-E, Supplementary file 1), and AFM data (Figure 4H-I). The use of a well-characterized bundling-defective mutant (Hertzog et al., 2010) provides mechanistic specificity. The dominant-negative effect in wild-type cells and the citation supporting Eps8 dimerization (Kishan et al., 1997) strengthen the interpretation.

results.result: Over-expression of α-actinin, another actin bundling protein, increases cortical tension and intracellular pressure by >50% and partially rescues leader bleb size and migration defects in Eps8-KD cells, though not to the same extent as Eps8 re-expression. This demonstrates that actin bundling is critical for leader bleb formation and cortical mechanics, but other Eps8 functions cannot be compensated by α-actinin.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by AFM data (Figure 4H-I), imaging data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and quantitative measurements (Figure 4C-E, Supplementary file 1). The partial rescue by α-actinin provides strong evidence for the importance of bundling activity while also revealing Eps8-specific functions. The comparison between α-actinin and Eps8 rescue is well-controlled.

results.result: The actin capping activity of Eps8 limits leader bleb size and antagonizes actin bundling at the bleb tip. A capping-defective mutant (Emerald-mEps8Δcap, V689D/L693D) forms significantly larger leader blebs, nearly doubles the proportion of migrating cells, and exhibits nearly fivefold higher actin bundle anisotropy at bleb tips compared to wild-type Eps8. The mutant decreases cortical actin density in the cell body but increases cortex tension and intracellular pressure. The capping-defective mutant is equally distributed along the leader bleb or concentrated at the tip, unlike wild-type Eps8 which forms a gradient.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C64 are supported by imaging data (Figure 5A-G, Video 5), quantitative measurements (Figure 5B-C, Supplementary file 1), anisotropy analyses (Figure 5G″), and AFM data (Figure 5H-I). The use of a well-characterized capping-defective mutant (Hertzog et al., 2010) provides mechanistic specificity. The opposing effects of the capping and bundling mutants provide strong evidence for antagonistic activities. C64 is appropriately labeled as speculation.

results.result: Erk activity is required for leader bleb formation and spatially regulates the actin cytoskeleton. U0126 (MEK/Erk inhibitor) inhibits Eps8 phosphorylation, reduces leader bleb area and cortical actin density, completely blocks leader bleb-based migration, and reduces cortex tension and intracellular pressure. U0126 treatment causes cells to form actin bundles in the cell center (lacking myosin II) and lamellipodia/filopodia at the periphery, indicating that Erk promotes cortical actin density while inhibiting central actin bundling.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C73 are supported by immunoprecipitation/Western blot data validating U0126 effects on Eps8 phosphorylation (Figure 6A), imaging data (Figure 6B-C, Video 6), quantitative measurements (Figure 6D-F), and AFM data (Figure 6G-H, Supplementary file 1). C65 is supported by citation to Menna et al., 2009. The spatial reorganization of the cytoskeleton upon Erk inhibition is well-documented and provides strong evidence for Erk's role in spatial regulation.

results.result: Erk phosphorylation sites S624 and T628 in Eps8 are required for leader bleb formation and migration. A non-phosphorylatable mutant (Emerald-mEps8-SATA, S624A/T628A) blocks leader bleb formation, reduces leader bleb size by ~50%, and strongly inhibits migration. The mutant forms thick actin bundles in the cell center that lack myosin II and are not labeled by F-tractin but are dense with phalloidin-stained actin. Over-expression induces central bundles in ~70% of cells versus ~30% for wild-type Eps8. These results suggest that S624/T628 phosphorylation suppresses central actin bundles, while other MEK/Erk targets regulate cortical actin density.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C85 are supported by imaging data (Figure 7A-G, Video 7), quantitative measurements (Figure 7B-D, H, Supplementary file 1), and phalloidin/vimentin staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The observation that F-tractin does not label the bundles while phalloidin does is intriguing; C79 appropriately speculates about competition for binding sites. The finding that Erk inhibition induces bundles regardless of S624A/T628A mutations (C86) provides important mechanistic insight.

results.result: Both capping and bundling activities are required for Erk inhibition-induced cable formation. Over-expression of either Emerald-mEps8Δcap or Emerald-mEps8Δbund does not induce cables with or without U0126. The capping-defective mutant cannot rescue leader bleb loss induced by U0126, indicating Erk promotes leader blebs through additional mechanisms beyond Eps8 capping regulation. Emerald-mEps8-SATA expression reduces cortex tension and intracellular pressure to levels similar to U0126 treatment. Together, these results suggest Erk-mediated phosphorylation of S624/T628 coordinates local co-regulation of Eps8 capping and bundling activities to control cortical mechanics and leader bleb formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C93 are supported by imaging data (Figure 7G-H, Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and AFM data (Figures 7I-J, Supplementary file 1). The requirement for both activities in cable formation is well-demonstrated. The failure of the capping-defective mutant to rescue U0126 effects (C88-C89) is important for understanding the complexity of Erk regulation. C91 appropriately speculates about indirect mechanisms. The AFM data (C92) provides quantitative support for the mechanistic model.

results.result: Erk activity is highly concentrated in leader blebs and forms a gradient with peak activity at the distal tip. Using the EKAREV FRET biosensor, Erk activity is low and diffuse in adherent cells but shows heightened FRET specifically in blebs of non-adherent cells, appearing as a flash just after protrusion and maintained until retraction. In confined cells, there is >250% enrichment of Erk activity in leader blebs relative to the cell body, with a shallow gradient peaking at the tip. Soluble proteins (EGFP, EKAREV, Erk, MEK, B-Raf) are enriched 10-20% in leader blebs, likely due to exclusion of membranous organelles.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C105 are supported by FRET imaging data (Figure 8A-G, Video 8) and quantitative measurements. The EKAREV biosensor is validated by U0126 treatment reducing FRET to minimal levels (C96, Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The >250% enrichment of Erk activity is much greater than the 10-20% enrichment of soluble proteins, indicating specific concentration of Erk activity rather than passive accumulation. Regional analysis provides spatial resolution of the gradient.

results.result: The bleb neck acts as a diffusion barrier that slows equilibration of soluble components between the leader bleb and cell body. Photo-conversion of mEos2 in the leader bleb shows that red fluorescence is retained within and diffuses throughout the leader bleb before equilibrating with the cell body. This suggests that Erk activity may be trapped in leader blebs by this diffusion barrier.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are supported by photo-conversion experiments (Figure 8H, Video 9). The observation that fluorescence is retained in the leader bleb provides direct evidence for restricted diffusion. C108 appropriately includes speculation ('may be trapped') about the mechanism for Erk activity concentration. The diffusion barrier concept is consistent with the observed protein enrichments.

results.result: A375 melanoma cells carry the B-Raf V600E mutation that activates the Raf/MEK/Erk pathway. This mutation is commonly found in melanoma, bypasses Ras and negative feedback, and predisposes cells to blebbing through a Raf/MEK/Erk/MLCK/RLC/myosin contractility cascade. Drugs targeting B-Raf V600E have short-term effects but are limited by compensatory pathway upregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C125-C128 are supported by citations to established literature (Davies et al., 2002; Logue and Morrison, 2012) and represent well-established knowledge about melanoma biology and the Erk pathway. These claims provide important context for the study but are not novel findings.

results.result: Eps8 plays a critical role in promoting cortex tension and intracellular pressure to drive the mesenchymal-to-leader bleb transition and rapid, adhesion-independent migration of confined cancer cells. Both contractility and proper cytoskeletal organization are critical for generating cortical mechanical properties conducive to leader bleb-based migration. The bundling activity of Eps8 promotes cortical inhomogeneity and cellular pressure that mediate symmetry breaking.
results.evaluation: Claims C109, C111-C113 are summary interpretations of the study's major findings, supported by the collective evidence from knockdown, rescue, mutant, and AFM experiments. C112 appropriately integrates the current findings with previous work (Bergert et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Ruprecht et al., 2015). These are well-supported conclusions from the data.

results.result: The authors propose a model where Eps8's bundling and capping activities act antagonistically, with capping down-regulation enhancing bundling efficiency. Local regulation of Eps8 capping activity by Erk could promote polarization with opposing gradients in actin density and bundling along the leader bleb. This gradient may organize cortical tension to maintain bleb shape and drive cortical flow, with increased tension at the tip opposed by myosin II contractility at the neck. The depletion of myosin II and actin at the bleb tip would allow intracellular pressure to drive membrane protrusion and migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C120 represent a speculative mechanistic model integrating the study's findings. While the model is consistent with the data (opposing effects of capping and bundling mutants, Erk gradient, spatial distributions of proteins), many aspects are not directly tested. C114 includes appropriate speculation ('may be'). C115-C120 are largely speculative about how the observed gradients translate into mechanical forces and migration. The model is plausible but requires further experimental validation.

results.result: Leader bleb-based migration may be relevant to cancer cell migration in vivo, including intraepithelial migration, perivascular spaces, between muscle fibers, and in solid tumors. Inhibition of Erk blocks leader bleb formation, consistent with the importance of Erk effectors like Eps8 in confined cancer cell migration. Eps8 is required for leader bleb-based migration in multiple cancer cell types (A375, U2OS, A549) with different oncogenic drivers. Targeting specific effectors like Eps8 rather than canonical signaling enzymes may have therapeutic value for preventing metastasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C131 represent discussion of potential in vivo relevance and therapeutic implications. C121 is supported by citation (Charras and Sahai, 2014). C123-C124 are supported by the U0126 and multi-cell-line data (Figure 2). However, C122, C130, and C131 are speculative about therapeutic applications without direct evidence. The multi-cell-line data (C129) strengthens the generalizability but in vivo relevance remains to be demonstrated.
